The C ommon-Ion E ffect

Suppose a small amount of NaCl(s) is added to a saturated solution of AgCl. What happens? Sodium chloride is quite soluble in water and dissolves to form Na1(aq) and Cl2(aq) ions, raising the concentration of chloride ion. The quantity Q0 5 [Ag1][Cl2] then exceeds the Ksp of silver chloride, and silver chloride precipitates until the concentrations of Ag1(aq) and Cl2(aq) are sufficiently reduced that the solubility product expression once again is satisfied.

The same equilibrium may be approached from the other direction. The amount of AgCl(s) that can dissolve in a solution of sodium chloride is less than the amount that could dissolve in the same volume of pure water. Because [Ag1][Cl2] 5 Ksp, a graph of the equilibrium concentration of silver ion against chloride concentration has the form of a hyperbola (Fig. 16.7).
